title: Loops
description: Repeat actions with for and while loops, control them with break and continue, and draw patterns.

subLevels.title: for loops
subLevels.summary: Repeat code a set number of times with for and range().

blocks.text: Imagine printing "Hello" five times. You could write print five times, but that gets boring fast, and what if you needed it 500 times?
A loop tells Python to repeat some lines for you.

items: Change one number to repeat more or fewer times
Loops are used in almost every real program

blocks.text: A loop repeats the indented lines underneath it.

explanation: range(5) means "do this 5 times".
i is the loop variable. Python gives it a new value on each repeat.
The line ends with a colon : and the repeated line is indented, just like if.

blocks.text: The loop variable holds the current number. range() can start and stop where you choose.

explanation: range(1, 6) starts at 1 and stops before 6.
So n is 1, then 2, 3, 4 and finally 5.
The third number is the step: jump by 2 each time.
10 is never printed because range stops before the end number.

blocks.text: You can use the loop variable in calculations. The * symbol multiplies.

explanation: num stays 3 the whole time.
i changes: 1, 2, 3, 4, 5.
The f-string works out num * i on every repeat.

blocks.title: Tip
blocks.text: Change num to 7 and you get the 7 times table. One change, five new lines.
A very common pattern: start a total at 0 and add to it on every repeat. total += n is a short way to write total = total + n.

blocks.code:
total = 0
for n in range(1, 5):
    total += n
print(total)
explanation: total starts at 0.
The loop adds 1, then 2, then 3, then 4.
print(total) is not indented, so it runs once, after the loop.

blocks.title: Common mistake
blocks.text: range(1, 5) gives 1, 2, 3, 4 — it stops BEFORE 5. If you want to include 5, write range(1, 6).

questions.explanation: range(0, 9, 3) starts at 0 and jumps by 3: 0, 3, 6. 9 is the stop number and range always stops before it, so 9 is not printed. The third number is the step, so it does not count 0, 1, 2.
questions.hint: Remember what each of the three numbers in range means, especially the stop number.
optionFeedback: This includes 9, but range always stops before the stop number, so 9 is left out.
range starts at the first number, which is 0 here, and it also stops before 9.
The third number is the step, so the loop jumps by 3 instead of counting by 1.
Right: it starts at 0, jumps by 3, and stops before 9, giving 0, 3, 6.

questions.explanation: range(start, stop) includes the start but stops before the stop number, so 6 is not included.
questions.hint: Think about which end of range() is included and which end is left out.
optionFeedback: Right: range includes the start, 2, and stops just before 6.
This includes 6, but range stops before the stop number.
range includes the start number, so the sequence begins at 2, not 3.
range gives every whole number from the start up to (but not including) the stop, not just the two ends.

questions.prompt: Find the bug in this loop.
options: The colon : is missing after range(3)
The loop variable must be called n
questions.explanation: Every for line ends with a colon, exactly like an if line. The name i is fine, and the body must be indented.
questions.hint: Compare this for line with the if lines you wrote in Level 2: how do they end?
optionFeedback: range() uses round brackets, exactly as in range(3); square brackets are not needed.
Right: every for line must end with a colon, just like an if line.
The loop variable can have any valid name; the lesson used i, n and others.
The body of a loop must be indented; removing the indent would break the code.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank so the loop prints the numbers 1 to 10.
questions.explanation: The stop number is never included, so to reach 10 you stop at 11. range(1, 10) would stop at 9.
questions.hint: Remember the common mistake tip about where range stops counting.
optionFeedback: Right: start at 1 and stop at 11, so the last number printed is 10.
range(1, 10) stops before 10, so it prints only 1 to 9.
range(0, 10) starts at 0 and stops before 10, so it adds 0 and misses 10.
range(10) also stops before 10, so 10 is never printed.

questions.explanation: total becomes 1, then 3, then 6. range(1, 4) gives 1, 2, 3 — it does not include 4, so the answer is not 10.
questions.code:
total = 0
for n in range(1, 4):
    total += n
print(total)
questions.hint: Track the value of total after each repeat, and list the numbers range(1, 4) gives.
optionFeedback: 10 would need 4 to be added too, but range(1, 4) stops before 4.
3 is only the last number the loop sees; total keeps adding every number, not just the last one.
Right: total goes 1, then 3, then 6.
total += n runs inside the loop on every repeat, so total does not stay at 0.

subLevels.title: while loops
subLevels.summary: Keep repeating while a condition is True.

blocks.text: A while loop keeps going as long as its condition is True. It checks the condition before every repeat.

explanation: count starts at 1.
Each repeat prints count and then adds 1 to it.
When count becomes 4, count <= 3 is False and the loop stops.

blocks.text: You can count down too. n -= 1 is short for n = n - 1.

blocks.code:
n = 3
while n > 0:
    print(n)
    n -= 1
print("Lift off!")
explanation: The loop runs while n is bigger than 0.
n goes 3, 2, 1, then 0 — and the loop stops.
The last print is not indented, so it runs after the loop.

pages.title: When you don't know how many times

blocks.text: Use while when you can't say in advance how many repeats you need. Here we double some savings until they reach 1000.

blocks.code:
savings = 100
years = 0
while savings < 1000:
    savings = savings * 2
    years += 1
print(f"{years} years, savings: {savings}")
explanation: 100 becomes 200, 400, 800 and then 1600.
years counts how many times the loop ran.

blocks.text: A while loop is also great for asking again until the answer is right:

blocks.code:
password = ""
while password != "python":
    password = input("Password: ")
print("Welcome!")
explanation: The loop keeps asking while the answer is not "python".
When the user types python, the condition is False and the loop ends.

blocks.text: If the condition never becomes False, the loop runs forever. This is called an infinite loop.

blocks.title: Common mistake
blocks.text: Forgetting to change the variable, for example leaving out count += 1, makes the condition stay True forever. In the Practical tab, press Stop if this happens.

items: Use for when you know how many repeats you need
Use while when you repeat until something changes

blocks.text: Every while loop needs something inside it that eventually makes the condition False.

questions.explanation: x is printed while it is less than 4: 1, 2, 3. When x becomes 4 the condition is False, so 4 is never printed.
questions.hint: Check the condition just before each repeat, especially when x has become 4.
optionFeedback: When x becomes 4, x < 4 is False, so the loop ends before printing 4.
Right: 1, 2 and 3 are printed, then x is 4 and the condition fails.
x starts at 1, and print runs before x += 1, so the first number shown is 1.
print is inside the loop, so it runs on every repeat, not only once at the end.

questions.prompt: When does a while loop stop?
options: When it reaches the last line of the file
questions.explanation: A while loop repeats as long as the condition is True and stops as soon as it is False. There is no built-in repeat limit.
questions.hint: Recall what a while loop checks before every single repeat.
optionFeedback: A while loop has no built-in repeat limit; it depends only on its condition.
It's the other way round: the loop keeps going while the condition is True.
Reaching the end of the loop body only sends Python back to check the condition again.
Right: the loop repeats while the condition is True and stops as soon as it is False.

questions.prompt: What is wrong with this code?
options: n never changes, so the loop runs forever
print can't be inside a while loop
questions.explanation: n stays 5, so n > 0 is always True. Adding n -= 1 inside the loop fixes it. range() is only used with for.
questions.hint: Follow the value of n through a few repeats and see whether it ever changes.
optionFeedback: range() is used with for loops; a while loop only needs a condition.
A single = stores a value; a condition needs a comparison such as >.
Right: nothing inside the loop changes n, so n > 0 stays True forever.
Any lines can go inside a while loop, including print; the lesson's countdown prints inside its loop.

questions.prompt: Which line, placed inside the loop, makes this countdown finish?
questions.explanation: n -= 1 makes n smaller each time until n > 0 is False. n += 1 counts up, so the loop would never end.
questions.hint: The condition is n > 0, so think about which direction n must move.
optionFeedback: Right: n -= 1 makes n smaller each time until n > 0 is False.
n += 1 makes n bigger, so n > 0 stays True and the loop never ends.
n = 3 resets n to the same value each time, so the loop never finishes.
== only compares and gives True or False; it does not change n.

questions.explanation: n goes 10, 7, 4, 1. At 1 the condition n > 3 is False, so the loop stops and prints 1. It does not stop at 4 because 4 > 3 is still True.
questions.hint: Write down n after each subtraction and check n > 3 every time.
optionFeedback: Right: n goes 10, 7, 4, 1, and only at 1 is n > 3 False.
At 4, the condition n > 3 is still True, so the loop subtracts 3 once more.
n never equals 3 here: it jumps from 4 straight down to 1.
7 is n after only the first repeat; 7 > 3 is True, so the loop keeps going.

options: A while loop always runs at least once
A while loop may run zero times if its condition starts False
while loops can only count upwards
You must know the number of repeats before using while
questions.explanation: The condition is checked before the first repeat, so a False condition means the body never runs.
questions.hint: Think about when the condition is checked: before or after the first repeat?
optionFeedback: The condition is checked before the first repeat, so a False start means the body never runs.
Right: if the condition is False at the start, the indented lines are skipped completely.
While loops can count down too, like the countdown that printed 3, 2, 1.
while is the loop to use when you don't know the number of repeats in advance.

subLevels.title: break and continue
subLevels.summary: Stop a loop early or skip a single repeat.

blocks.text: break jumps out of the loop straight away, even if there are repeats left.

explanation: The loop would normally run up to 9.
When n is 4, break ends the loop before print(n).
Python carries on with the line after the loop.

blocks.text: continue skips the rest of the current repeat and moves to the next one. The % symbol gives the remainder of a division: 7 % 2 is 1, 8 % 2 is 0. So n % 2 == 0 means n is even.

explanation: For even numbers, continue skips print(n).
The loop does not stop — it just moves on.

blocks.text: break = leave the loop. continue = skip to the next repeat.

pages.title: break in a while True loop

blocks.text: while True: repeats forever, so you use break to get out. This is handy when the stopping point is decided in the middle of the loop.

explanation: total grows 5, 10, 15, 20.
When it reaches 20, break ends the loop.

blocks.title: Common mistake
blocks.text: A while True loop with no break inside runs forever. Also make sure break is indented inside the if, otherwise the loop stops on the very first repeat.

questions.explanation: When n is 3, break ends the loop before print runs, so only 1 and 2 are shown. break does not skip just one number — it stops the loop.
questions.hint: Notice that the if with break comes before print inside the loop.
optionFeedback: Right: when n is 3, break ends the loop before print runs.
break runs before print(n) when n is 3, so 3 is never shown.
The numbers before 3 are printed first; break only stops what comes after.
Skipping one number and carrying on is what continue does; break leaves the loop entirely.

questions.explanation: continue skips only the repeat where n is 2. The loop keeps going, so 3 and 4 are still printed. Stopping after 1 is what break would do.
questions.hint: Remember the key point: one keyword leaves the loop, the other skips a repeat.
optionFeedback: When n is 2, continue jumps past print, so 2 is not shown.
Stopping after 1 is what break would do; continue lets the loop keep going.
n is 1 on the first repeat and the if is False, so 1 is printed.
Right: only the repeat where n is 2 is skipped.

options: Restarts the loop from the very first number
Skips the rest of this repeat and moves on to the next one
questions.explanation: continue only skips the current repeat. Stopping the loop completely is what break does.
questions.hint: Look at the odd numbers example and notice which numbers were missing.
optionFeedback: Stopping the loop completely is what break does.
continue moves on to the next number; it never goes back to the start.
Right: continue skips the rest of the current repeat and moves to the next one.
Waiting for the user is what input() does; continue doesn't wait for anything.

questions.explanation: % gives the remainder: 7 divided by 3 is 2 with 1 left over. 2 is how many times 3 fits, not the remainder.
questions.hint: Think of the leftover after sharing seven sweets equally between three friends.
optionFeedback: 2 is how many times 3 fits into 7; % gives what is left over instead.
Right: 3 fits into 7 twice (6), leaving a remainder of 1.
% does not give a decimal answer; it gives the whole-number remainder.
21 is 7 times 3; the % symbol means remainder, not multiply.

subLevels.title: Nested loops and patterns
subLevels.summary: Put a loop inside a loop to make grids and shapes.

blocks.text: A nested loop is a loop inside another loop. For every single repeat of the outer loop, the inner loop runs all the way through.

explanation: The outer loop runs 2 times (row 0 and row 1).
Each time, the inner loop runs 3 times (col 0, 1, 2).
2 x 3 = 6 lines in total.

blocks.text: print normally moves to a new line. Add end=" " to print a space instead. An empty print() just moves to the next line.

blocks.code:
for i in range(3):
    print(i, end=" ")
print()
print("next line")
explanation: end=" " keeps all three numbers on the same line.
print() on its own finishes that line.

blocks.text: Multiplying a string by a number repeats it.

blocks.title: Tip
blocks.text: This only works with a whole number: "ab" * 3 is fine, "ab" * "3" is an error.

blocks.code:
for row in range(1, 5):
    print("*" * row)
explanation: row goes 1, 2, 3, 4.
Each line prints that many stars.

blocks.text: The same shape with numbers, using a real nested loop:

explanation: The inner loop runs row times.
print() after the inner loop starts the next line.
a picks the row, b picks the column.
Each cell is a * b.

blocks.text: Total repeats of the inner body = outer repeats x inner repeats.
With nested loops, the indentation of each line decides which loop it belongs to. Move a line left or right and the output changes completely.

explanation: print() is not indented, so it runs only once, after both loops.
All 9 stars end up on one line.

blocks.title: Common mistake
blocks.text: To get 3 rows of ***, the final print() must be indented one level, inside the outer loop but outside the inner loop.

questions.prompt: How many times is hi printed?
questions.explanation: The inner loop runs 4 times for each of the 3 outer repeats: 3 x 4 = 12. Adding them (7) is a common mix-up.
questions.hint: Count how many times the inner loop runs for each single outer repeat.
optionFeedback: 7 adds the two counts, but the inner loop runs fully for every outer repeat, so you multiply.
Right: 4 inner repeats for each of 3 outer repeats is 3 x 4 = 12.
4 is just one pass of the inner loop; it runs again for every outer repeat.
3 counts only the outer repeats, but print is inside the inner loop.

questions.explanation: r goes 1, 2, 3 and each line prints r hashes, so the triangle grows downward.
questions.code:
for r in range(1, 4):
    print("#" * r)
questions.hint: Work out what r is on each repeat, then how many hashes that line gets.
optionFeedback: r starts at 1 and grows, so the first line is the shortest.
Right: r is 1, 2, 3, so each line has one more # than the last.
"#" * r repeats the hash r times, so the lines grow longer.
print runs inside the loop, once per repeat, so there are three lines, not one.

questions.prompt: What does end=" " do in print(x, end=" ")?
options: Prints a space instead of moving to a new line
Adds a blank line after the value
questions.explanation: end sets what is printed after the value. By default it's a new line; end=" " swaps it for a space.
questions.hint: Recall what print normally does straight after it shows a value.
optionFeedback: Right: end=" " puts a space after the value instead of a new line.
end is a setting of print, not a command to stop the program.
end=" " removes the move to a new line; it does not add an extra blank line.
end is a setting name, not text in quotes, so the word end is never printed.

questions.explanation: A string times a whole number repeats the string, with no spaces added.
questions.hint: Recall what multiplying a string by a whole number does.
optionFeedback: * with a string repeats it; it does not stick the number on the end.
Repeating a string adds no spaces between the copies.
A string times a whole number is allowed; only a string times a string causes an error.
Right: "ab" is repeated 3 times with nothing in between.

questions.prompt: This should draw 3 rows of ***, but prints all stars on one line. Why?
options: end="" is not allowed in a loop
The inner loop must use a different range
print() is not indented inside the outer loop
questions.explanation: print() runs only once, after both loops. Indent it inside the outer loop so each row ends with a new line.
questions.hint: Look at how far the final print() is indented compared with each loop.
optionFeedback: end="" is allowed anywhere; it just keeps the stars on the same line.
Both ranges are fine; the problem is where the new line is printed, not how many stars there are.
Right: print() runs only once after both loops, so indent it inside the outer loop.
Changing to range(4) would just print more stars, still all on one line.

questions.explanation: The pairs are (0,0), (0,1), (1,0), (1,1), and their sums are 0, 1, 1, 2.
questions.hint: List every pair of i and j in order, then add each pair.
optionFeedback: This counts up by one, but i and j only go up to 1, so the biggest sum is 1 + 1.
That only covers pairs where i and j are equal; the inner loop runs fully for each i.
Right: the pairs are (0,0), (0,1), (1,0), (1,1), giving 0, 1, 1, 2.
Both loops start at 0, so the first sum is 0 + 0, not 1.

questions.prompt: To print 1 2 3 on one line, what goes in the blank? print(n, ____)
questions.explanation: end=" " replaces the new line with a space. Writing just " " prints a space as a second value but still moves to a new line every time, and print has no space or line setting.
questions.hint: Think about the print setting that replaces the usual move to a new line.
optionFeedback: Right: end=" " replaces the new line with a space, so 1 2 3 stay on one line.
print has no space setting; the setting that controls what comes after the value is end.
A plain " " is printed as a second value, but print still moves to a new line each time.
print has no line setting, so this would cause an error.

questions.prompt: Which statement about nested loops is true?
options: The outer loop finishes before the inner loop starts
Both loops always run the same number of times
The inner loop can't use the outer loop's variable
The inner loop runs completely for every repeat of the outer loop
questions.explanation: For each outer repeat, the inner loop starts again and runs to the end. The inner loop can use the outer variable, as in range(row).
questions.hint: Remember how 0 0, 0 1, 0 2 all printed before row changed to 1.
optionFeedback: The inner loop runs inside each outer repeat, so the outer loop can't finish first.
Each loop has its own range, so they can repeat different numbers of times, like 2 and 3 in the example.
The inner loop can use the outer variable, as in for col in range(row).
Right: for each outer repeat, the inner loop starts again and runs to the end.

projects.title: Number Guessing Game
projects.summary: Give the player five tries to guess a secret number, with hints and stars.

briefing.title: Build a Number Guessing Game
text: The computer thinks of a number from 1 to 10. The player has five tries and gets a hint after each wrong guess.
Fewer guesses earn more stars. A for loop counts the tries and break stops it early.
why: Games are a fun way to see loops in action
It combines for, range(), break, conditions and repeating text with *
briefing.sampleOutput:
I'm thinking of a number from 1 to 10.
Guess 1: 4
Too low!
Guess 2: 9
Too high!
Guess 3: 7
Correct! You got it in 3 tries.
Stars: ***

finalCode: print("I'm thinking of a number from 1 to 10.")
print(f"Correct! You got it in {attempt} tries.")

stages.title: Set up the game
stages.instruction: The secret number and the number of tries are ready. Add a variable that remembers whether the player has won yet.

question.prompt: Which line sets up the 'has won' flag?
question.explanation: A Boolean flag starts as False and is switched to True when something happens (1.3).

optionFeedback: "False" in quotes is text, and any non-empty text counts as True in an if.
A Boolean flag starts as False and is switched to True when something happens (1.3).
== compares instead of storing, and won doesn't exist yet: a NameError.
The player hasn't won before the game even starts.

stages.title: Count the tries
stages.instruction: Repeat the guessing once for each try, numbering the tries 1 to 5.

question.prompt: Which loop gives attempt the values 1, 2, 3, 4, 5?
question.explanation: range(1, 6) starts at 1 and stops before 6, so it gives 1 to 5 (3.1).

optionFeedback: range(5) gives 0 to 4, so the first guess would be called Guess 0.
range(1, 6) starts at 1 and stops before 6, so it gives 1 to 5 (3.1).
range(1, 5) stops before 5: only four tries.
attempt doesn't exist before the loop, so this is a NameError.

stages.title: Read a guess
stages.instruction: Inside the loop, ask for a guess, showing which try it is, and turn it into a number.

question.explanation: The f-string shows the try number, and int() makes the answer a number (1.4).

optionFeedback: The f-string shows the try number, and int() makes the answer a number (1.4).
The guess stays text, so guess == secret would never be True.
Without the f, the prompt literally shows {attempt}.
One closing bracket is missing. This is a SyntaxError.

stages.title: A correct guess
stages.instruction: If the guess matches the secret, remember the win and stop asking.

question.prompt: What should happen when the guess is right?
options: Use continue to go to the next guess
Set won to True and keep looping
Set won to False, then break out of the loop
Set won to True, then break out of the loop
question.explanation: break ends the loop at once, so no more guesses are asked for (3.3).

optionFeedback: continue skips to the next try, so the player keeps guessing after winning.
The player would be asked again even after getting it right.
won would stay False, so the program would say they lost.
break ends the loop at once, so no more guesses are asked for (3.3).

stages.title: Give a hint
stages.instruction: For a wrong guess, tell the player whether to go higher or lower.

question.prompt: Which line checks for a guess that is too low?
question.explanation: If the guess is smaller than the secret, it's too low (2.1, 2.3).

optionFeedback: This checks for too high, but prints Too low!
The colon is missing. This is a SyntaxError.
If the guess is smaller than the secret, it's too low (2.1, 2.3).
The operator is <=, not =<. This is a SyntaxError.

stages.title: Award stars
stages.instruction: After the loop, if the player won, print how many tries it took and one star for every try left, plus one.

question.explanation: "*" * 3 repeats the star three times (3.4). The brackets do the maths first.

optionFeedback: "*" * 3 repeats the star three times (3.4). The brackets do the maths first.
You can't + text and a number. This is a TypeError.
This repeats the word Stars: three times instead.
Without brackets, "*" * 5 runs first, then text minus a number is a TypeError.

stages.title: Out of tries
stages.instruction: Finish with an else that runs when the player didn't win.

question.prompt: When does the else part run?
options: Only when the first guess is right
When all five tries were used without guessing the number
question.explanation: won stays False only if the loop ran out without a correct guess (2.2).

optionFeedback: This else belongs to if won after the loop, not to the hints inside it.
A right guess sets won to True, so the if part runs instead.
won stays False only if the loop ran out without a correct guess (2.2).
break only runs after a correct guess. Five wrong guesses never reach it.

walkthrough: won starts as False. The for loop gives attempt the values 1 to 5.
Each try reads a number. A correct guess sets won to True and break stops the loop.
Wrong guesses get a hint from elif / else.
After the loop, if won prints the result and "*" * 3 draws three stars for a 3rd-try win.

cheatSheet.title: Loops

items.note: range(start, stop, step). stop is never included.

items.code:
total = 0
for n in range(1, 5):
    total += n
print(total)
items.note: Add up with a running total.
Repeats while the condition is True. Change the variable!
break stops the loop at once.
continue skips to the next repeat.

items.code:
for row in range(1, 4):
    print("*" * row)

items.note: end=" " stays on the same line.

remember: A while loop must change something, or it never ends.
